title: Elvis Presley rightsholders sue Anthropic for $41M over 274 songs
subtitle: ABG EPE IP, representing the Presley estate and co-plaintiffs including Abilene Music and Raleigh Music Publishing, allege Claude was trained on and continues to output protected lyrics — and ask the court to purge them from training data and model weights.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Authentic Brands Group's ABG EPE IP LLC, acting for the Elvis Presley estate, filed a federal copyright suit against Anthropic PBC in the US District Court for the Northern District of California on October 23. The case is docketed 5:26-cv-12473. The complaint lists 274 compositions and seeks statutory damages at the maximum $150,000 per infringed work, which sets the baseline exposure at roughly $41 million; one summary of the filing reads the arithmetic higher, closer to $48.6 million. Co-plaintiffs include Abilene Music, Raleigh Music Publishing, trusts tied to the Aberbach family, and the Luigi Creatore Trust.

The complaint brings three counts: direct copyright infringement, circumvention of technological protection measures under 17 U.S.C. § 1201, and removal or alteration of copyright management information. Plaintiffs allege that even after Anthropic added lyric-related guardrails in response to the Music Publishers' earlier suit, newer Claude releases still reproduce protected lyrics on request. The requested remedy includes an order to purge the unlicensed lyrics from Anthropic's training data and model weights — a technical ask that no court has yet granted at frontier-model scale and that, if ordered, would effectively force retraining.

This is the first major music-publishing copyright case against Anthropic since the 2023 Music Publishers suit (filed by Universal, Concord, and ABKCO), which is still in discovery. What distinguishes the Presley filing is the catalog's cultural weight combined with the targeted DMCA § 1201 and § 1202 claims, which are harder to defend on fair-use grounds than straight § 501 infringement. If plaintiffs prove that Claude's lyric-blocking guardrails qualify as 'technological protection measures' that the system itself routes around, the legal theory applies to every frontier model — and the surgical-weight-removal remedy becomes the operational threat.

A note for learners: the training-data copyright wars are entering a new phase. The question is shifting from 'is training fair use' to 'what counts as a technological protection measure inside a model, and what has to be purged if you lose.' For anyone working on dataset provenance, filtering, or model editing, the engineering problem is becoming legal infrastructure. Learn how memorization is measured and how weight-level unlearning actually works — not because it is interesting, but because courts are starting to order it.
